name: Transnational Business Law
profile: This course introduces students to the legal frameworks governing business transactions in a globalized economy. It examines how law shapes cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, and digital commerce. Emphasis is placed on the practical application of legal rules to real-world business scenarios, as well as on comparative and international perspectives. Through interactive class discussions, problem - based assignments, quizzes, and an arbitration simulation, students develop the analytical and practical skills needed to identify legal risks and design effective solutions in transnational business contexts.

name: Law, Society & Justice
profile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.

name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.

name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
profile: This course provides students insights into the main legal issues in the fields of criminal law and criminal justice. We will discuss the concepts of criminal accountability, differentiated types of ‘guilt’, the essentials of justifications and excuse, the importance of the legality principle and other fundamental considerations, such as the ‘presumption of innocence’. Students are also introduced to interdisciplinary research into organized crime. The main guiding principles of criminal law and criminal justice will be presented and investigated and the moral and legal debate on the justification of punishment and on recent developments in criminal law will be considered. Special attention will be paid to legal skills, such as reading legal texts, analyzing criminal case law and formulating a normative opinion, based on legally and morally sound argumentation. Students apply theory and skills in a simulated legal aid clinic.

name: Introduction to Public International Law
profile: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.

name: Comparative Constitutional Law
profile: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.

name: Principles of Private Law
profile: Life comprises a variety of situations in which private law plays a role . Simply considering the home implicates several complex relationships: family relatives , landlords and tenants, neighbors. Stepping out the front door leads to a further range of transactions that can have legal consequences for those involved. The rights and obligations associated with relationships and transactions among (natural and legal) persons are largely determined by a collection of legal areas known collectively as private law. This course introduces students to principles of selected fields of private law, and students will closely examine property law, tort law, contract law, and other legal areas. The overarching principles within each of these fields will be illuminated using a comparative law approach, considering primarily the legal systems of Germany, France, England, China, and the United States of America. Additionally, students will be challenged to consider private law concepts in broader contexts. Building on the skills acquired in GOSLAWJ101 and other UCR law track courses , this course on private law will seek to uncover the latent social, economic, and political pressures underlying many of the legal principles that will be discussed.

name: Foundations of European Union Law
profile: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
